{{Short description|Mathematical method in elliptic functions}}
'''Landen's transformation''' is a mapping of the parameters of an [[elliptic integral]], useful for the efficient numerical evaluation of elliptic functions. It was originally due to [[John Landen]] and independently rediscovered by [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gauss|first1=C. F.|last2=Nachlass|title=Arithmetisch geometrisches Mittel, Werke, Bd. 3|journal=Königlichen Gesell. Wiss., Göttingen|date=1876|pages=361–403}}</ref>

== Statement ==

The [[Elliptic integral#Incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind|incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind]] {{math|F}} is 
:<math> F(\varphi \setminus \alpha) = F(\varphi, \sin \alpha) = \int_0^\varphi \frac{d \theta}{\sqrt{1-(\sin \theta \sin \alpha)^2}},</math>
where <math>\alpha</math> is the [[Angular eccentricity|modular angle]]. Landen's transformation states that if <math>\alpha_0</math>, <math>\alpha_1</math>, <math>\varphi_0</math>, <math>\varphi_1</math> are such that <math>(1 + \sin\alpha_1)(1 + \cos\alpha_0) = 2</math> and <math>\tan(\varphi_1 - \varphi_0) = \cos\alpha_0 \tan \varphi_0</math>, then<ref>{{AS ref}}</ref>
:<math>\begin{align}
F(\varphi_0 \setminus \alpha_0) &= (1 + \cos\alpha_0)^{-1} F(\varphi_1 \setminus \alpha_1) \\
&= \tfrac{1}{2}(1 + \sin\alpha_1) F(\varphi_1 \setminus \alpha_1).
\end{align}</math>
Landen's transformation can similarly be expressed in terms of the elliptic modulus <math>k = \sin\alpha</math> and its complement <math>k' = \cos\alpha</math>.

==Complete elliptic integral==

In Gauss's formulation, the value of the integral
:<math>I = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 \cos^2(\theta) + b^2 \sin^2(\theta)}} \, d \theta</math>
is unchanged if <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are replaced by their [[arithmetic mean|arithmetic]] and [[geometric mean]]s respectively, that is
:<math>a_1 = \frac{a + b}{2},\qquad b_1 = \sqrt{a b},</math>
:<math>I_1 = \int _0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{a_1^2 \cos^2(\theta) + b_1^2 \sin^2(\theta)}} \, d \theta.</math>
Therefore,
:<math>I=\frac{1}{a}K\left(\frac{\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}{a}\right),   </math>
:<math>I_1=\frac{2}{a+b}K\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right).  </math>
From Landen's transformation we conclude
:<math>K\left(\frac{\sqrt{a^2 - b^2}}{a}\right)=\frac{2a}{a+b}K\left(\frac{a-b}{a+b}\right) </math>
and <math>I_1=I</math>.

===Proof===

The transformation may be effected by [[integration by substitution]]. It is convenient to first cast the integral in an [[algebraic function|algebraic]] form by a substitution of <math>\theta = \arctan (x/b)</math>, <math>d \theta = (\cos^{2}(\theta)/b) d x</math> giving

:<math>I = \int _0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 \cos^2(\theta) + b^2 \sin^2(\theta)}} \, d \theta = \int _0^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{(x^2 + a^2) (x^2 + b^2)}} \, dx</math>

A further substitution of <math>x = t + \sqrt{t^{2} + a b}</math> gives the desired result

:<math>\begin{align}I & = \int _0^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{(x^2 + a^2) (x^2 + b^2)}} \, dx \\
 & = \int _{- \infty}^\infty \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{\left( t^2 + \left( \frac{a + b}{2}\right)^2 \right) (t^2 + a b)}} \, dt \\
 & = \int _0^\infty\frac{1}{\sqrt{\left( t^2 + \left( \frac{a + b}{2}\right)^2\right) \left(t^2 + \left(\sqrt{a b}\right)^2\right)}} \, dt \end{align}</math>

This latter step is facilitated by writing the radical as

:<math>\sqrt{(x^2 + a^2) (x^2 + b^2)} = 2x \sqrt{t^2 + \left( \frac{a + b}{2}\right)^2}</math>

and the infinitesimal as

:<math> dx = \frac{x}{\sqrt{t^2 + a b}} \, dt</math>

so that the factor of <math>x</math> is recognized and cancelled between the two factors.

{{hidden begin 
| title = {{pad|3em}} ''Details of the derivation''
| bodystyle = font-size: 100%
| toggle = left
}}
To prove 
<math display=block>\left(x^2+a^2\right)\left(x^2+b^2\right) = 4\,x^2\left( t^2+\left( \frac{a+b}{2} \right)^2 \right)</math>
we write <math display=inline>x=t+r</math> with <math display=inline>r=\sqrt{t^2+ab}</math>. We also write <math display=inline>\bar{x}=t-r</math>. Then
<math display=block>x^2\bar{x}^2 = a^2b^2</math>
since <math display=inline>x\bar{x} = t^2-r^2 = -ab</math>, and
<math display=block>x^2+\bar{x}^2 = 2\,\left(t^2+r^2\right) = 4\,t^2+2ab.</math>
Then 
<math display=block>\begin{aligned}\left(x^2+a^2\right)\left(x^2+b^2\right) &= x^2\left(x^2+a^2+b^2+\frac{a^2b^2}{x^2} \right)\\
&= x^2\left(x^2+\bar{x}^2+a^2+b^2\right)\\
&= x^2\left(4\,t^2+2ab+a^2+b^2\right)\\
&= 4\,x^2\left( t^2+\left( \frac{a+b}{2} \right)^2 \right)\end{aligned}</math>
{{hidden end}}

===Arithmetic-geometric mean and Legendre's first integral===

If the transformation is iterated a number of times, then the parameters <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> converge very rapidly to a common value, even if they are initially of different orders of magnitude. The limiting value is called the [[arithmetic-geometric mean]] of <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>, <math>\operatorname{AGM}(a,b)</math>. In the limit, the integrand becomes a constant, so that integration is trivial

:<math>I = \int _0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 \cos^2(\theta) + b^2 \sin^2(\theta)}} \, d\theta = \int _0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\frac{1}{\operatorname{AGM}(a,b)} \, d\theta = \frac{\pi}{2 \operatorname{AGM}(a,b)}</math>

The integral may also be recognized as a multiple of [[Legendre form|Legendre's complete elliptic integral of the first kind]]. Putting <math>b^2 = a^2 (1 - k^2)</math>

:<math>I = \frac{1}{a} \int _0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - k^2 \sin^2(\theta)}} \, d\theta = \frac{1}{a} F\left( \frac{\pi}{2},k\right) = \frac{1}{a} K(k)</math>

Hence, for any <math>a</math>, the arithmetic-geometric mean and the complete elliptic integral of the first kind are related by

:<math>K(k) = \frac{\pi }{2 \operatorname{AGM}(1, \sqrt{1 - k^2})}</math>

By performing an inverse transformation (reverse arithmetic-geometric mean iteration), that is

:<math>a_{-1} = a + \sqrt{a^2 - b^2} \, </math>

:<math>b_{-1} = a - \sqrt{a^2 - b^2} \, </math>

:<math>\operatorname{AGM}(a,b) = \operatorname{AGM}\left(a + \sqrt{a^2 - b^2},a - \sqrt{a^2 - b^2}\right) \, </math>

the relationship may be written as

:<math>K(k) = \frac{\pi}{2 \operatorname{AGM}(1 + k, 1 - k)} \, </math>

which may be solved for the AGM of a pair of arbitrary arguments;

:<math> \operatorname{AGM}(u,v) = \frac{\pi (u + v)}{4 K\left( \frac{u - v}{v + u}\right)}.</math>
